about: Statistical Methods in Economics (ECON0005) is a 15-credit, Term 1 module that is compulsory for first-year single-honours Economics students at UCL (2026/27 module catalogue). It runs from probability, random variables and distributions through the law of large numbers and central limit theorem to estimation, hypothesis testing and an introduction to the linear regression model, taught through lectures and tutorials, and it introduces the statistics package Stata. The 2026/27 catalogue lists assessment as an exam (70%) and in-class activity (30%), and ECON0002 must be taken at the same time.
topics: Law of large numbers and central limit theorem

notes.body:
Probability is the language the rest of the module (and all of econometrics) is written in, so the definitions need to be exact.

Set-up:
- Sample space S: the set of all possible outcomes of an experiment.
- Event: a subset of S. Aᶜ is the complement, A ∩ B the intersection ("both"), A ∪ B the union ("at least one").
- Mutually exclusive (disjoint) events: A ∩ B = ∅, so they cannot happen together.

The axioms (Kolmogorov):
- P(A) ≥ 0 for every event A.
- P(S) = 1.
- For mutually exclusive events A₁, A₂, …, the probability of their union is the sum of their probabilities.

Everything else follows from these:
- P(Aᶜ) = 1 − P(A), and P(∅) = 0.
- Addition rule: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B). The intersection is subtracted because it would otherwise be counted twice.
- If outcomes are equally likely, P(A) = (number of outcomes in A) / (number in S).

Counting:
- Ordered selections of k from n without replacement: n!/(n − k)!.
- Unordered selections (combinations): C(n, k) = n!/(k!(n − k)!). For example C(5, 2) = 10.

Conditional probability: for P(B) > 0, P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B). Rearranging gives the multiplication rule P(A ∩ B) = P(A | B)P(B).

Independence: A and B are independent if P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B); when P(B) > 0 this is the same as P(A | B) = P(A). Do not confuse independence with mutual exclusivity: if A and B are mutually exclusive and both have positive probability, then P(A ∩ B) = 0 ≠ P(A)P(B), so they are dependent (knowing one happened tells you the other did not).

Law of total probability: if B₁, …, Bₖ partition S (disjoint, and together they cover S), then P(A) = Σ P(A | Bᵢ)P(Bᵢ).

Bayes' theorem: P(B | A) = P(A | B)P(B) / P(A), with P(A) found from the law of total probability.

Worked example (a screening test):
- 1% of firms are in financial distress (D). A warning indicator flags 95% of distressed firms and wrongly flags 5% of healthy ones.
- P(flag) = 0.95 × 0.01 + 0.05 × 0.99 = 0.0095 + 0.0495 = 0.059.
- P(D | flag) = 0.0095/0.059 ≈ 0.161.
- So only about 16% of flagged firms are actually distressed, because healthy firms are so much more common. Mixing up P(flag | D) = 0.95 with P(D | flag) is the classic error (sometimes called the base-rate fallacy).

Exam tips: write down the events and the given probabilities in symbols before calculating; draw a tree diagram for multi-stage problems; and always check whether a question says "independent" or "mutually exclusive", because they lead to very different calculations.

A random variable X is a function that assigns a number to each outcome in the sample space. It turns events into numbers we can average.

Describing a random variable:
- Discrete X: probability mass function p(x) = P(X = x), with p(x) ≥ 0 and Σ p(x) = 1.
- Continuous X: probability density function f(x) ≥ 0 with ∫ f(x) dx = 1 over the whole line. Probabilities are areas: P(a ≤ X ≤ b) = ∫ from a to b of f(x) dx, and P(X = a) = 0 for any single value.
- Cumulative distribution function (cdf): F(x) = P(X ≤ x), non-decreasing from 0 to 1. For continuous X, f(x) = F′(x) wherever the derivative exists.

Expectation (mean):
- Discrete: E[X] = Σ x p(x). Continuous: E[X] = ∫ x f(x) dx.
- E[g(X)] = Σ g(x) p(x) (or the integral version). In general E[g(X)] ≠ g(E[X]); for example E[X²] ≠ (E[X])² unless X is constant.
- Linearity: E[aX + b] = aE[X] + b, and E[X + Y] = E[X] + E[Y] for any X and Y (independence not needed).

Variance and standard deviation:
- Var(X) = E[(X − μ)²] = E[X²] − μ², where μ = E[X]. SD = √Var(X).
- Var(aX + b) = a²Var(X). Adding a constant shifts the distribution but does not change its spread.

Two variables:
- Joint distribution of (X, Y); marginal distributions are found by summing (or integrating) out the other variable.
- Covariance: Cov(X, Y) = E[(X − μ_X)(Y − μ_Y)] = E[XY] − E[X]E[Y].
- Correlation: ρ = Cov(X, Y)/(SD(X)SD(Y)), always between −1 and 1, and unit-free.
- Var(X + Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y) + 2Cov(X, Y); Var(X − Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y) − 2Cov(X, Y).
- If X and Y are independent, then E[XY] = E[X]E[Y] and Cov(X, Y) = 0. The converse is false: let X take −1, 0, 1 with equal probability and Y = X². Then Cov(X, Y) = E[X³] − E[X]E[X²] = 0, yet Y is completely determined by X.
- Conditional expectation E[Y | X] is the mean of Y for a given value of X. The law of iterated expectations, E[Y] = E[E[Y | X]], is used constantly in regression.

Worked example: X takes values 0, 1, 2 with probabilities 0.2, 0.5, 0.3.
- E[X] = 0(0.2) + 1(0.5) + 2(0.3) = 1.1.
- E[X²] = 0 + 1(0.5) + 4(0.3) = 1.7.
- Var(X) = 1.7 − 1.1² = 0.49, so SD = 0.7.
- If Y = 3X + 2: E[Y] = 5.3 and Var(Y) = 9 × 0.49 = 4.41.

Exam tips: lay out a table of x, p(x), x p(x) and x² p(x) for discrete calculations; remember the constant in a linear transformation disappears from the variance and the multiplier is squared.

A handful of distributions do most of the work in economics and econometrics. For each, know when it applies, its formula, its mean and its variance.

Discrete distributions:
- Bernoulli(p): X = 1 with probability p and 0 otherwise. Mean p, variance p(1 − p).
- Binomial(n, p): number of successes in n independent trials, each with the same success probability p. P(X = k) = C(n, k)pᵏ(1 − p)ⁿ⁻ᵏ for k = 0, 1, …, n. Mean np, variance np(1 − p). It is a sum of n independent Bernoulli(p) variables.
- Poisson(λ): counts of events in a fixed interval when events occur independently at a constant average rate λ. P(X = k) = e^(−λ)λᵏ/k! for k = 0, 1, 2, …. Mean and variance are both λ. It approximates Binomial(n, p) when n is large and p small, with λ = np.

Continuous distributions:
- Uniform(a, b): density 1/(b − a) on [a, b]. Mean (a + b)/2, variance (b − a)²/12.
- Exponential(λ): density λe^(−λx) for x ≥ 0. Mean 1/λ, variance 1/λ². It is memoryless: P(X > s + t | X > s) = P(X > t).
- Normal N(μ, σ²): bell-shaped and symmetric about μ. About 68%, 95% and 99.7% of the probability lies within 1, 2 and 3 standard deviations of the mean (more precisely, 95% within 1.96σ).
- Standardising: if X ~ N(μ, σ²) then Z = (X − μ)/σ ~ N(0, 1), so all normal probabilities come from the standard normal table Φ(z) = P(Z ≤ z).
- A linear function of a normal variable is normal, and a sum of independent normal variables is normal.

Distributions built from the normal (used for inference later):
- Chi-squared with k degrees of freedom, χ²(k): the sum of squares of k independent N(0, 1) variables. Mean k.
- Student's t(k): Z/√(V/k) where Z ~ N(0, 1) and V ~ χ²(k) are independent. Symmetric with fatter tails than the normal; tends to N(0, 1) as k grows.
- F(k₁, k₂): ratio of two independent chi-squared variables, each divided by its degrees of freedom.

Worked examples:
- Binomial: n = 10 trials, p = 0.3. P(X = 2) = C(10, 2)(0.3)²(0.7)⁸ = 45 × 0.09 × 0.0576 ≈ 0.2335. Mean 3, variance 2.1.
- Poisson: calls arrive at an average of 3 per hour. P(no calls in an hour) = e^(−3) ≈ 0.0498; P(exactly 2) = e^(−3) × 9/2 ≈ 0.2240.
- Normal: X ~ N(100, 15²). P(X > 130) = P(Z > (130 − 100)/15) = P(Z > 2) = 1 − Φ(2) ≈ 0.0228.

Exam tips: always standardise using the standard deviation (not the variance); sketch the normal curve and shade the area you want before reading the table; check the binomial conditions (fixed n, independence, constant p) before using it.

notes.h: Law of large numbers and central limit theorem
notes.body:
These two results explain why sample averages are useful: the law of large numbers says the sample mean homes in on the population mean, and the central limit theorem says how it is distributed around it.

Two inequalities:
- Markov: if X ≥ 0 and a > 0, then P(X ≥ a) ≤ E[X]/a.
- Chebyshev: if X has finite mean μ and finite variance σ², then for any k > 0, P(|X − μ| ≥ kσ) ≤ 1/k². With k = 2 the bound is 0.25, whatever the distribution. (For a normal variable the true probability is only about 0.0455, so the bound is conservative but always valid.)

The sample mean of an iid sample:
- If X₁, …, Xₙ are independent and identically distributed (iid) with mean μ and variance σ², then X̄ₙ = (1/n)ΣXᵢ has E[X̄ₙ] = μ and Var(X̄ₙ) = σ²/n.
- The standard deviation of X̄ₙ, σ/√n, is called the standard error. It shrinks with √n, not n.

Weak law of large numbers (WLLN):
- Statement: if X₁, X₂, … are iid with mean μ and finite variance σ², then for every ε > 0, P(|X̄ₙ − μ| > ε) → 0 as n → ∞. We say X̄ₙ converges in probability to μ (plim X̄ₙ = μ).
- Proof sketch: by Chebyshev, P(|X̄ₙ − μ| > ε) ≤ Var(X̄ₙ)/ε² = σ²/(nε²) → 0. (Stronger versions need only a finite mean, but the finite-variance version is the one proved with Chebyshev.)
- Meaning: an estimator that converges in probability to the true parameter is called consistent.

Central limit theorem (CLT, Lindeberg–Lévy form):
- Statement: if X₁, X₂, … are iid with mean μ and variance σ², where 0 < σ² < ∞, then √n(X̄ₙ − μ)/σ converges in distribution to N(0, 1) as n → ∞.
- Practical use: for large n, X̄ₙ is approximately N(μ, σ²/n), whatever the shape of the population distribution.
- How large is large? A common rule of thumb is n ≥ 30, but heavily skewed populations need more. If the population itself is normal, X̄ₙ is exactly normal for every n.
- Normal approximation to the binomial: a Binomial(n, p) count is a sum of n Bernoulli variables, so for large n it is approximately N(np, np(1 − p)). A continuity correction (e.g. P(X ≥ 90) ≈ P(Y ≥ 89.5)) improves accuracy.

Worked example: individual spending has mean £50 and standard deviation £10. For a random sample of n = 100, the standard error is 10/√100 = 1. By the CLT, P(X̄ > 52) ≈ P(Z > (52 − 50)/1) = P(Z > 2) ≈ 0.0228.

Why it matters: confidence intervals and hypothesis tests later in the module (and the large-sample theory of regression) rely on the CLT to justify using normal critical values.

Exam tips: be precise about what converges to what (the LLN is about X̄ₙ approaching μ; the CLT is about the distribution of the standardised mean); state the iid and finite-variance conditions; remember to use σ/√n, not σ, when finding probabilities for a sample mean.

Statistics turns data into statements about the population that generated them. The key idea is that a statistic computed from a random sample is itself a random variable with its own distribution.

Vocabulary:
- Population: the full group (or the probability distribution) we care about; parameters such as μ and σ² describe it.
- Random sample: X₁, …, Xₙ independent and identically distributed (iid) draws from the population.
- Statistic: any function of the sample (for example the sample mean). An estimator is a statistic used to estimate a parameter; an estimate is its value in a particular sample.

Descriptive statistics:
- Location: sample mean x̄ = (1/n)Σxᵢ; median (the middle ordered value), which is robust to outliers.
- Spread: sample variance s² = Σ(xᵢ − x̄)²/(n − 1); sample standard deviation s; range; interquartile range (upper quartile minus lower quartile).
- Shape: skewness (right-skewed data such as incomes usually have mean above median).
- Two variables: sample covariance and sample correlation, and scatter plots.

Why divide by n − 1?
- The deviations from x̄ always sum to zero, so only n − 1 of them are free: one degree of freedom is used up estimating μ by x̄.
- With n − 1, E[S²] = σ², so S² is unbiased. Dividing by n gives an estimator whose expectation is ((n − 1)/n)σ², biased downwards.

Sampling distributions (iid sample, mean μ, variance σ²):
- E[X̄] = μ and Var(X̄) = σ²/n.
- If the population is normal: X̄ ~ N(μ, σ²/n) exactly; (n − 1)S²/σ² ~ χ²(n − 1); X̄ and S² are independent; and T = (X̄ − μ)/(S/√n) ~ t(n − 1).
- Replacing the unknown σ by S is what turns the normal into the t distribution. For large n the t(n − 1) distribution is close to N(0, 1).
- Without normality, the CLT still makes X̄ approximately normal for large n.

Worked example: data 3, 5, 7, 9, 11.
- x̄ = 35/5 = 7.
- Deviations −4, −2, 0, 2, 4; squared deviations sum to 40.
- s² = 40/4 = 10, s ≈ 3.16. (Dividing by n would give 8.)
- Estimated standard error of the mean: s/√n = 3.16/√5 ≈ 1.41.

Software: the module introduces Stata. Basic commands you will meet in any introduction include summarize (means, standard deviations, minimum and maximum; add the detail option for percentiles), tabulate (frequency tables), histogram, generate (create new variables) and describe (list variables). Use the materials and do-files your class provides for the exact commands expected.

Exam tips: distinguish clearly between a parameter (fixed, unknown), an estimator (a random variable) and an estimate (a number); show the n − 1 explicitly; and say which result relies on normality and which relies on the CLT.

A point estimator gives a single best guess for a parameter; an interval estimator gives a range with a stated level of confidence.

Properties of point estimators (θ̂ estimating θ):
- Unbiased: E[θ̂] = θ. Bias = E[θ̂] − θ.
- Efficient (relative): among unbiased estimators, the one with the smaller variance is more efficient.
- Mean squared error: MSE(θ̂) = E[(θ̂ − θ)²] = Var(θ̂) + (Bias)². A slightly biased estimator can have lower MSE than an unbiased one.
- Consistent: θ̂ converges in probability to θ as n → ∞. A sufficient condition is that both the bias and the variance tend to zero.

Example: estimating μ from an iid sample.
- X̄ is unbiased with variance σ²/n.
- X₁ (just the first observation) is also unbiased, but its variance is σ² whatever the sample size. It is less efficient than X̄ and not consistent.
- Among all linear unbiased estimators Σaᵢxᵢ of μ, the sample mean has the smallest variance.

Methods of finding estimators: the method of moments sets sample moments equal to population moments and solves (for example, estimating p in a Bernoulli model by the sample proportion). Maximum likelihood chooses the parameter value that maximises the likelihood of the observed sample (its probability, or density for continuous data). The 2026/27 catalogue topic list does not name maximum likelihood, so follow your lecture notes for whether and how far it is covered.

Confidence intervals for a mean:
- σ known and population normal: x̄ ± z_(α/2) × σ/√n, exact for any n. For 95%, z = 1.96.
- n large (any population with finite variance): the same formula with s in place of σ is approximately valid, by the CLT.
- σ unknown and population normal: x̄ ± t_(n−1, α/2) × s/√n.
- Proportion (large n): p̂ ± z_(α/2)√(p̂(1 − p̂)/n).

Worked example: n = 25 from a normal population, x̄ = 12, s = 5.
- Standard error: 5/√25 = 1.
- t with 24 degrees of freedom, upper 2.5% point ≈ 2.064.
- 95% CI: 12 ± 2.064 = (9.94, 14.06).

Interpreting a confidence interval:
- Correct: if we repeated the sampling many times, about 95% of intervals built this way would contain the true μ.
- Incorrect: "there is a 95% probability that μ lies in (9.94, 14.06)". In the classical (frequentist) approach μ is fixed; it is the interval that is random.

What changes the width:
- Higher confidence → wider interval (larger critical value).
- More variable population → wider.
- Larger n → narrower, but only at rate 1/√n: to halve the width you need four times the sample size.

Exam tips: state which formula you are using and why (σ known or not, normality, large n); give the degrees of freedom for t; and write a one-sentence interpretation in context, avoiding the "probability μ is in this interval" wording.

A hypothesis test asks whether the data are consistent with a specific claim about a parameter.

The ingredients:
- Null hypothesis H₀: the claim being tested, e.g. H₀: μ = 10.
- Alternative H₁: two-sided (μ ≠ 10) or one-sided (μ > 10 or μ < 10). Choose it before seeing the data.
- Test statistic: measures how far the estimate is from the null value in standard-error units, e.g. t = (x̄ − μ₀)/(s/√n).
- Rejection (critical) region: values of the statistic so extreme that we reject H₀.
- Significance level (size) α: the probability of rejecting H₀ when it is true, typically 5% or 1%.

Two kinds of error:
- Type I error: rejecting H₀ when it is true. Probability α.
- Type II error: failing to reject H₀ when it is false. Probability β.
- Power = 1 − β = probability of rejecting H₀ when it is false. Power rises with the sample size, with the distance between the true value and μ₀, and with α; it falls as σ rises.
- For a fixed n, reducing α increases β: there is a trade-off.

p-values:
- The p-value is the probability, calculated assuming H₀ is true, of obtaining a test statistic at least as extreme as the one observed.
- Reject H₀ at level α if p < α.
- It is not the probability that H₀ is true.

Common tests:
- Mean, σ known and population normal (exact), or n large using s in place of σ (approximate, by the CLT): z = (x̄ − μ₀)/(σ/√n), compared with N(0, 1).
- Mean, small n, normal population, σ unknown: t with n − 1 degrees of freedom.
- Proportion: z = (p̂ − p₀)/√(p₀(1 − p₀)/n).
- Difference in means of two independent samples: (x̄₁ − x̄₂)/√(s₁²/n₁ + s₂²/n₂) for large samples.

Link with confidence intervals: a two-sided test at level α rejects H₀: μ = μ₀ exactly when μ₀ lies outside the (1 − α) confidence interval built with the same standard error and critical value.

Worked example: H₀: μ = 10 against H₁: μ ≠ 10. n = 64, x̄ = 11.2, s = 4.
- Standard error = 4/√64 = 0.5; z = (11.2 − 10)/0.5 = 2.4.
- Two-sided p-value = 2(1 − Φ(2.4)) ≈ 2 × 0.0082 = 0.0164.
- Reject at 5% (p < 0.05) but not at 1%.
- Power if the true mean were 11 (5% test): reject if |x̄ − 10| > 1.96 × 0.5 = 0.98. P(x̄ > 10.98 | μ = 11) = P(Z > −0.04) ≈ 0.516 (the lower tail adds almost nothing), so power is about 0.52.

In Stata, a one-sample t-test of whether a variable's mean equals 10 can be run with ttest followed by the variable name and == 10.

Language matters: say "we reject H₀" or "we do not reject H₀ at the 5% level", not "we accept H₀". And remember statistical significance is not the same as economic importance: a tiny effect can be significant in a huge sample.

Exam tips: always write H₀, H₁, the statistic and its distribution under H₀, the critical value or p-value, and a conclusion in words.

The module ends by introducing the tool at the heart of econometrics: the simple linear regression model.

The model: yᵢ = β₀ + β₁xᵢ + uᵢ, for i = 1, …, n.
- y is the dependent variable, x the explanatory variable, u the error (everything else affecting y).
- β₁ is the change in y for a one-unit change in x, holding u fixed.

Ordinary least squares (OLS): choose b₀ and b₁ to minimise the sum of squared residuals Σ(yᵢ − b₀ − b₁xᵢ)². Setting the two partial derivatives to zero gives:
- β̂₁ = Σ(xᵢ − x̄)(yᵢ − ȳ) / Σ(xᵢ − x̄)², the sample covariance of x and y divided by the sample variance of x.
- β̂₀ = ȳ − β̂₁x̄.

Algebraic properties of OLS:
- The residuals ûᵢ = yᵢ − β̂₀ − β̂₁xᵢ sum to zero.
- The residuals have zero sample covariance with x.
- The fitted line passes through (x̄, ȳ).

Goodness of fit: SST = Σ(yᵢ − ȳ)² splits into explained SSE = Σ(ŷᵢ − ȳ)² and residual SSR = Σûᵢ². R² = SSE/SST = 1 − SSR/SST, the share of the sample variation in y explained by x. In simple regression R² equals the squared sample correlation between x and y.

Assumptions for unbiasedness:
- Linear in parameters; random sample; sample variation in x (not all xᵢ equal).
- Zero conditional mean: E[u | x] = 0. This is the crucial one. If an omitted factor in u is correlated with x, OLS is biased (omitted variable bias).
- Under these, E[β̂₁] = β₁.
- Adding homoskedasticity, Var(u | x) = σ², gives Var(β̂₁) = σ²/Σ(xᵢ − x̄)². σ² is estimated by σ̂² = SSR/(n − 2), because two parameters have been estimated.

Inference: t = (β̂₁ − b)/se(β̂₁) tests H₀: β₁ = b. If, in addition to the assumptions above, the errors are homoskedastic and normally distributed, it has a t distribution with n − 2 degrees of freedom; in large samples it is approximately N(0, 1).

Worked example: (x, y) = (1, 2), (2, 4), (3, 5), (4, 4), (5, 5).
- x̄ = 3, ȳ = 4. Σ(x − x̄)(y − ȳ) = 6, Σ(x − x̄)² = 10.
- β̂₁ = 0.6, β̂₀ = 4 − 0.6 × 3 = 2.2. Fitted line ŷ = 2.2 + 0.6x.
- SST = 6, SSR = 2.4, so R² = 0.6.
- σ̂² = 2.4/3 = 0.8; se(β̂₁) = √(0.8/10) ≈ 0.283; t ≈ 2.12 < 3.182 (t₃, 5%), so not significant at 5% with only five observations.

Interpretation with logs: if y is log(wage) and x is years of schooling, 100β₁ is approximately the percentage change in wage per extra year (exactly 100(e^β₁ − 1)%).

Correlation is not causation: β̂₁ estimates a causal effect only if E[u | x] = 0 is believable.

In Stata, regress y x reports the coefficients, standard errors, t statistics, p-values, confidence intervals and R².

Exam tips: show the means and the two sums before dividing; interpret coefficients in units of the data; and discuss whether the zero conditional mean assumption is plausible.

cards.b: P(A) ≥ 0 for every event; P(S) = 1; and for mutually exclusive events the probability of the union equals the sum of the probabilities.

cards.f: Addition rule for any two events
cards.b: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B). The intersection is subtracted so it is not counted twice.
P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B), defined when P(B) > 0.
A and B are independent if P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B); equivalently P(A | B) = P(A) when P(B) > 0.

cards.f: Can two mutually exclusive events with positive probabilities be independent?
cards.b: No. Then P(A ∩ B) = 0 but P(A)P(B) > 0, so the product rule fails: knowing A happened tells you B did not.
If B₁, …, Bₖ partition the sample space, P(A) = Σ P(A | Bᵢ)P(Bᵢ).
P(B | A) = P(A | B)P(B)/P(A), with P(A) usually found by the law of total probability.

cards.f: Number of ways to choose k items from n, ignoring order

cards.b: A function that assigns a real number to each outcome in the sample space.
F(x) = P(X ≤ x). It is non-decreasing, tends to 0 as x → −∞ and to 1 as x → +∞.
Var(X) = E[X²] − (E[X])².
a²Var(X): the additive constant b has no effect on spread, and the multiplier is squared.
Var(X) + Var(Y) + 2Cov(X, Y). The covariance term drops out only if X and Y are uncorrelated.
No. Independence implies zero covariance, but not the reverse: e.g. X uniform on {−1, 0, 1} and Y = X² have Cov = 0 yet are dependent.
E[Y] = E[E[Y | X]]: averaging the conditional means of Y over the distribution of X gives the overall mean of Y.
Between −1 and 1 inclusive; ±1 only when Y is an exact linear function of X.
P(X = k) = C(n, k)pᵏ(1 − p)ⁿ⁻ᵏ; mean np; variance np(1 − p).
A fixed number n of trials, each with two outcomes, independent of each other, with the same success probability p.
P(X = k) = e^(−λ)λᵏ/k! for k = 0, 1, 2, …; mean λ and variance λ.
Mean (a + b)/2; variance (b − a)²/12.
If X ~ N(μ, σ²) then Z = (X − μ)/σ ~ N(0, 1). Divide by the standard deviation σ, not the variance.

cards.f: Chi-squared distribution with k degrees of freedom
cards.b: The distribution of the sum of squares of k independent standard normal variables; its mean is k.

cards.f: Student's t distribution with k degrees of freedom
cards.b: Z/√(V/k) with Z ~ N(0, 1) independent of V ~ χ²(k). Symmetric, fatter-tailed than N(0, 1), and tends to N(0, 1) as k → ∞.
P(X > s + t | X > s) = P(X > t). Among continuous distributions, only the exponential has it.
If X has finite mean μ and variance σ², then P(|X − μ| ≥ kσ) ≤ 1/k² for any k > 0.
If X ≥ 0 and a > 0, then P(X ≥ a) ≤ E[X]/a.

cards.f: Mean and variance of the sample mean (iid sample)
cards.b: E[X̄] = μ and Var(X̄) = σ²/n, so the standard error is σ/√n.
If X₁, X₂, … are iid with mean μ (and finite variance), then P(|X̄ₙ − μ| > ε) → 0 for every ε > 0: X̄ₙ converges in probability to μ.
If X₁, X₂, … are iid with mean μ and finite variance σ² > 0, then √n(X̄ₙ − μ)/σ converges in distribution to N(0, 1).

cards.f: Is X̄ exactly normal for small n?
cards.b: Only if the population is normal. Otherwise normality is an approximation that improves as n grows (CLT).
An estimator that converges in probability to the true parameter value as the sample size grows.
When approximating a discrete count by a normal, widen by 0.5: e.g. P(X ≥ 90) ≈ P(Y ≥ 89.5) for the approximating normal Y.
Observations X₁, …, Xₙ that are independent and identically distributed (iid) draws from the population distribution.
An estimator is a rule (a random variable, a function of the sample); an estimate is the number it gives for one particular sample.
s² = Σ(xᵢ − x̄)²/(n − 1).

cards.f: Why n − 1 in the sample variance?
cards.b: Deviations from x̄ sum to zero, so one degree of freedom is lost; dividing by n − 1 makes E[S²] = σ² (unbiased).

cards.f: Distribution of (X̄ − μ)/(S/√n) for a normal population
cards.b: Student's t with n − 1 degrees of freedom.

cards.f: Distribution of (n − 1)S²/σ² for a normal population
cards.b: Chi-squared with n − 1 degrees of freedom.

cards.f: Standard error of the sample mean
cards.b: σ/√n, estimated by s/√n when σ is unknown.

cards.f: Mean vs median in right-skewed data
cards.b: In right-skewed data (e.g. incomes) the mean is usually above the median, because a few large values pull the mean up.
θ̂ is unbiased for θ if E[θ̂] = θ for every value of θ.
MSE(θ̂) = Var(θ̂) + (Bias(θ̂))².
If bias → 0 and variance → 0 as n → ∞, then θ̂ converges in probability to θ, so it is consistent.

cards.f: 95% CI for μ, normal population, σ unknown
Correct interpretation of a 95% confidence interval
cards.b: In repeated samples, about 95% of intervals constructed this way would contain the true parameter.

cards.f: How must n change to halve the width of a CI?
cards.b: Multiply n by 4, because the width is proportional to 1/√n.

cards.f: Why is X₁ alone a poor estimator of μ?
cards.b: It is unbiased but its variance stays σ² as n grows, so it is less efficient than X̄ and not consistent.
Set sample moments (e.g. the sample mean) equal to the corresponding population moments and solve for the parameters.
Rejecting H₀ when H₀ is true. Its probability is the significance level α.
Failing to reject H₀ when H₀ is false. Its probability is β.
1 − β: the probability of rejecting H₀ when it is false. Increases with n, effect size and α.
The probability, computed assuming H₀ is true, of a test statistic at least as extreme as the one observed.
Reject H₀ at significance level α if p < α.
Reject H₀: μ = μ₀ at 5% (two-sided) exactly when μ₀ lies outside the 95% confidence interval built the same way.
t = (x̄ − μ₀)/(s/√n), with n − 1 degrees of freedom under H₀ for a normal population.
A statistically significant effect may be too small to matter economically; a large effect may be insignificant in a small, noisy sample.
β̂₁ = Σ(xᵢ − x̄)(yᵢ − ȳ)/Σ(xᵢ − x̄)², the sample covariance of x and y over the sample variance of x.
β̂₀ = ȳ − β̂₁x̄, so the fitted line passes through (x̄, ȳ).
R² = SSE/SST = 1 − SSR/SST: the fraction of the sample variation in y explained by the regression.

cards.f: Key assumption for unbiasedness of OLS
cards.b: Zero conditional mean: E[u | x] = 0 (with linearity, random sampling and variation in x).
If a factor in the error term affects y and is correlated with x, then E[u | x] ≠ 0 and OLS is biased.
Var(u | x) = σ² for all x: the error variance does not depend on x.

cards.f: Estimator of the error variance in simple regression
cards.b: σ̂² = SSR/(n − 2); two degrees of freedom are lost estimating β₀ and β₁.

cards.f: Two algebraic properties of OLS residuals
cards.b: They sum to zero, and they have zero sample covariance with the regressor x.

questions.q: 1% of firms are distressed. An indicator flags 95% of distressed firms and 5% of healthy firms. A firm is flagged. What is the probability it is distressed?
options: About 0.161
questions.why: P(flag) = 0.95 × 0.01 + 0.05 × 0.99 = 0.059, so P(distressed | flag) = 0.0095/0.059 ≈ 0.161. The value 0.95 is P(flag | distressed), the conditional the wrong way round. 0.0095 is the joint probability P(distressed and flagged), which has not been divided by P(flag). 0.059 is P(flag) itself, the denominator rather than the answer.

questions.q: A and B are independent with P(A) = 0.5 and P(B) = 0.4. What is P(A ∪ B)?
questions.why: By independence P(A ∩ B) = 0.5 × 0.4 = 0.2, so P(A ∪ B) = 0.5 + 0.4 − 0.2 = 0.7. 0.9 adds the probabilities without subtracting the overlap, which is only valid for mutually exclusive events. 0.2 is the intersection, not the union. 0.8 is 1 − P(A)P(B), the probability that A and B do not both happen, which is a different event.

questions.q: Define what it means for events A and B to be independent. Prove that if A and B are independent then A and Bᶜ are also independent.
markScheme: States P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B) as the definition
Writes A as the disjoint union (A ∩ B) ∪ (A ∩ Bᶜ), so P(A ∩ Bᶜ) = P(A) − P(A ∩ B)
Substitutes independence: P(A) − P(A)P(B) = P(A)(1 − P(B))
Uses 1 − P(B) = P(Bᶜ) to conclude P(A ∩ Bᶜ) = P(A)P(Bᶜ)
questions.modelAnswer: A and B are independent if P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B). The events A ∩ B and A ∩ Bᶜ are disjoint and their union is A, so by the additivity axiom P(A) = P(A ∩ B) + P(A ∩ Bᶜ). Hence P(A ∩ Bᶜ) = P(A) − P(A ∩ B) = P(A) − P(A)P(B) = P(A)(1 − P(B)) = P(A)P(Bᶜ), which is the definition of independence for A and Bᶜ.

questions.q: X takes values 0, 1, 2 with probabilities 0.2, 0.5, 0.3, so E[X] = 1.1 and E[X²] = 1.7. What is Var(3X + 2)?
questions.why: Var(X) = 1.7 − 1.1² = 0.49, and Var(3X + 2) = 3² × 0.49 = 4.41. 1.47 multiplies the variance by 3 instead of 9 (the multiplier was not squared). 6.41 adds the constant 2 to the variance, but shifting a variable does not change its spread. 15.3 is 9 × E[X²], using the raw second moment instead of the variance.

questions.q: Which statement about random variables X and Y is always true?
options: If Cov(X, Y) = 0, then X and Y are independent
If X and Y are independent, then Cov(X, Y) = 0
If X and Y are independent, then Var(X − Y) = Var(X) − Var(Y)
E[XY] = E[X]E[Y] for any X and Y
questions.why: Independence gives E[XY] = E[X]E[Y], so the covariance is zero. The reverse implication fails (X uniform on −1, 0, 1 with Y = X² has zero covariance but Y depends on X). For independent variables Var(X − Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y): variances add even when the variables are subtracted, because Var(−Y) = Var(Y). E[XY] = E[X]E[Y] holds only when the variables are uncorrelated, not for every pair.

questions.q: Starting from Var(X) = E[(X − μ)²], show that Var(X) = E[X²] − μ². Hence find the variance of X where P(X = 0) = 0.2, P(X = 1) = 0.5, P(X = 2) = 0.3.
markScheme: Expands (X − μ)² = X² − 2μX + μ²
Uses linearity: E[X²] − 2μE[X] + μ² = E[X²] − μ²
questions.modelAnswer: Expanding, (X − μ)² = X² − 2μX + μ². Taking expectations and using linearity (μ is a constant), E[(X − μ)²] = E[X²] − 2μE[X] + μ² = E[X²] − 2μ² + μ² = E[X²] − μ². For the given distribution, E[X] = 0(0.2) + 1(0.5) + 2(0.3) = 1.1 and E[X²] = 0(0.2) + 1(0.5) + 4(0.3) = 1.7. So Var(X) = 1.7 − 1.21 = 0.49 (standard deviation 0.7).

questions.q: X ~ Binomial(10, 0.3). What is P(X = 2), to 4 decimal places?
questions.why: P(X = 2) = C(10, 2)(0.3)²(0.7)⁸ = 45 × 0.09 × 0.05765 ≈ 0.2335. 0.0052 is (0.3)²(0.7)⁸ without the binomial coefficient, i.e. the probability of one particular ordering. 0.3828 is the cumulative probability P(X ≤ 2). 0.0014 is 45 × (0.3)⁸(0.7)², which swaps the exponents and so gives P(X = 8).

The standard deviation is √225 = 15, so z = (130 − 100)/15 = 2 and P(Z > 2) = 1 − 0.9772 = 0.0228. 0.9772 is Φ(2) = P(X < 130), the wrong tail. 0.4470 comes from dividing by the variance 225 instead of the standard deviation (z ≈ 0.133). 0.0455 is P(|Z| > 2), the two-tailed probability, which wrongly adds the lower tail P(Z < −2) as well.

questions.q: Calls to a helpline arrive independently at an average rate of 3 per hour. Using a Poisson model, find (a) the probability of no calls in an hour, (b) the probability of exactly 2 calls, and (c) the mean and variance of the number of calls.
markScheme: Identifies X ~ Poisson(3)
Mean = variance = 3
questions.modelAnswer: Let X be the number of calls in an hour, X ~ Poisson(λ = 3). (a) P(X = 0) = e^(−3) ≈ 0.0498. (b) P(X = 2) = e^(−3) × 3²/2! = 4.5e^(−3) ≈ 0.2240. (c) For a Poisson distribution the mean and the variance both equal λ, so both are 3.

questions.q: Weekly earnings have mean £20 and standard deviation £6. Using the central limit theorem, what is the approximate probability that the mean of a random sample of 36 workers is below £19?
options: Approximately 0
questions.why: The standard error is 6/√36 = 1, so z = (19 − 20)/1 = −1 and P(Z < −1) ≈ 0.1587. 0.4338 uses the population standard deviation 6 instead of the standard error (z ≈ −0.167). 0.8413 is P(Z < 1), the wrong tail. Approximately 0 comes from dividing by n instead of √n (6/36 gives z = −6).

questions.q: Which statement is what the central limit theorem says?
options: For iid draws with finite positive variance, the distribution of √n(X̄ − μ)/σ approaches N(0, 1) as n grows
For large n, the sample mean is approximately normal only if the population itself is normal
As n grows, the individual observations in the sample become normally distributed
As n grows, the sample mean converges in probability to the population mean
questions.why: The CLT concerns the distribution of the standardised sample mean. The individual observations keep whatever distribution the population has; only the mean becomes approximately normal. Convergence of X̄ to μ is the law of large numbers, a different theorem. Saying that even a large-sample mean is approximately normal only for a normal population contradicts the CLT, which gives approximate normality for any population with finite positive variance (exact normality for every n does require a normal population, but that is a different claim).

questions.q: A random variable X has mean 80 and standard deviation 8. Use Chebyshev's inequality to bound P(|X − 80| ≥ 16). Compare this with the probability if X were normal, and explain the difference.
markScheme: Chebyshev bound 1/k² = 0.25
If normal, P(|Z| ≥ 2) ≈ 0.0455
Explains Chebyshev holds for every distribution with finite variance, so it is conservative
questions.modelAnswer: 16 is k = 2 standard deviations, so Chebyshev gives P(|X − 80| ≥ 16) ≤ 1/2² = 0.25. If X were normal, P(|Z| ≥ 2) = 2(1 − Φ(2)) ≈ 0.0455. The Chebyshev figure is much larger because it must hold for every distribution with that mean and variance, including very heavy-tailed ones; it uses only μ and σ, so it is a valid but conservative bound.

questions.q: What is the sample variance of the data 3, 5, 7, 9, 11?
questions.why: The mean is 7 and the squared deviations sum to 16 + 4 + 0 + 4 + 16 = 40, so s² = 40/(5 − 1) = 10. 8 divides by n = 5 instead of n − 1. 3.16 is √10, the sample standard deviation rather than the variance. 40 is the sum of squared deviations before dividing.

questions.q: A sample of n = 12 comes from a normal population with unknown variance. Why is (X̄ − μ)/(S/√n) compared with a t distribution rather than N(0, 1)?
options: Because the median rather than the mean is being used
Because σ has been replaced by the sample standard deviation S, which adds extra variability
Because the population is not normal
Because the sample size is more than 30
questions.why: With σ known the statistic would be exactly N(0, 1); estimating σ by S adds randomness, and the result is t with n − 1 = 11 degrees of freedom. Non-normality is not the reason: the exact t result actually requires a normal population. A sample size above 30 is when the t and normal become close, so it is not a reason to use t. The statistic uses the mean, not the median.

questions.q: Explain why the sample variance divides by n − 1 rather than n, and state the expected value of the estimator that divides by n.
markScheme: Deviations from x̄ sum to zero, so only n − 1 are free (one degree of freedom used estimating μ)
Using x̄ instead of μ makes Σ(xᵢ − x̄)² systematically smaller than Σ(xᵢ − μ)²
E[Σ(Xᵢ − X̄)²] = (n − 1)σ², so dividing by n − 1 gives E[S²] = σ² (unbiased)
Dividing by n gives expectation ((n − 1)/n)σ², a downward bias that vanishes as n grows
questions.modelAnswer: Because x̄ is chosen from the same data, the deviations xᵢ − x̄ always sum to zero, so only n − 1 of them can vary freely: one degree of freedom is used up in estimating μ. The sum of squared deviations about x̄ is also never larger than the sum about μ, so it understates the spread. One can show E[Σ(Xᵢ − X̄)²] = (n − 1)σ², so S² = Σ(Xᵢ − X̄)²/(n − 1) is unbiased for σ². The estimator that divides by n has expectation ((n − 1)/n)σ², which is biased downwards, though the bias disappears as n → ∞.

questions.q: A sample of n = 25 from a normal population gives x̄ = 12 and s = 5. The t critical value with 24 degrees of freedom is 2.064. What is the 95% confidence interval for μ?
questions.why: The standard error is 5/√25 = 1, so the interval is 12 ± 2.064 = (9.94, 14.06). (10.04, 13.96) uses the normal value 1.96, which ignores that σ is estimated from a small sample. (11.59, 12.41) divides s by n = 25 instead of √25 (standard error 0.2). (1.68, 22.32) uses s = 5 itself instead of the standard error.

questions.q: A 95% confidence interval for mean household saving is (£9.94, £14.06). Which interpretation is correct?
options: The sample mean lies in this interval with probability 0.95
There is a 95% probability that the true mean lies between £9.94 and £14.06
If the sampling were repeated many times, about 95% of intervals built this way would contain the true mean
95% of households in the sample saved between £9.94 and £14.06
questions.why: The 95% describes the long-run success rate of the method. Once computed, this particular interval either contains the fixed true mean or does not, so assigning it a 95% probability treats the parameter as random. The interval concerns the population mean, not the spread of individual households. The sample mean is the centre of the interval, so it always lies inside it.

questions.q: Let X₁, …, Xₙ be an iid sample with mean μ and variance σ². Compare the estimators X̄ and X₁ for μ in terms of bias, variance and consistency. Which would you use?
markScheme: Both unbiased: E[X̄] = μ and E[X₁] = μ
Var(X̄) = σ²/n; Var(X₁) = σ²
X̄ more efficient for n > 1
X̄ consistent (variance → 0, so plim X̄ = μ by the LLN); X₁ not consistent
Conclusion: use X̄
questions.modelAnswer: Both are unbiased: E[X̄] = (1/n)ΣE[Xᵢ] = μ and E[X₁] = μ. Their variances differ: Var(X̄) = σ²/n while Var(X₁) = σ². For n > 1, X̄ has the smaller variance and so is more efficient. As n → ∞, Var(X̄) → 0 and by the law of large numbers X̄ converges in probability to μ, so it is consistent; X₁ ignores the extra data, its distribution never changes, and it is not consistent. X̄ is therefore preferred.

questions.q: Testing H₀: μ = 10 against H₁: μ ≠ 10 with n = 64, x̄ = 11.2 and s = 4, using the normal approximation. What is the p-value?
questions.why: z = (11.2 − 10)/(4/√64) = 2.4, and the two-sided p-value is 2(1 − Φ(2.4)) ≈ 0.0164. 0.0082 is the one-tail probability, which is not doubled for a two-sided alternative. 0.9918 is Φ(2.4), the probability below the statistic rather than beyond it. 0.7642 comes from using s = 4 instead of the standard error 0.5 (z = 0.3).

questions.q: What is a Type I error?
options: Rejecting H₀ when H₀ is false
Concluding the p-value is the probability that H₀ is true
Rejecting H₀ when H₀ is true
Failing to reject H₀ when H₀ is false
questions.why: A Type I error is a false rejection, and its probability is α. Failing to reject a false H₀ is a Type II error. Rejecting a false H₀ is a correct decision, and its probability is the power. Reading the p-value as the probability that H₀ is true is a common misinterpretation, not a type of testing error.

questions.q: A sample of 16 observations from a normal population has x̄ = 52 and s = 6. Test H₀: μ = 50 against H₁: μ ≠ 50 at the 5% level (t₁₅ critical value 2.131). State your conclusion.
markScheme: States H₀ and H₁ and uses a t test because σ is unknown and n is small
Standard error = 6/√16 = 1.5
Compares |t| = 1.33 with 2.131 (15 df)
Does not reject H₀ at 5%; data consistent with μ = 50
questions.modelAnswer: H₀: μ = 50, H₁: μ ≠ 50. σ is unknown and n is small, so use t = (x̄ − μ₀)/(s/√n), which has a t distribution with 15 degrees of freedom under H₀. The standard error is 6/√16 = 1.5 and t = 2/1.5 ≈ 1.33. Since |1.33| < 2.131 we do not reject H₀ at the 5% level (the two-sided p-value is about 0.20). The sample does not provide significant evidence that the mean differs from 50.

questions.q: For the data (1, 2), (2, 4), (3, 5), (4, 4), (5, 5), Σ(x − x̄)(y − ȳ) = 6, Σ(x − x̄)² = 10 and Σ(y − ȳ)² = 6. What is the OLS slope from regressing y on x?
questions.why: β̂₁ = Σ(x − x̄)(y − ȳ)/Σ(x − x̄)² = 6/10 = 0.6. 1.0 divides by the variation in y (6/6), which is the slope of the reverse regression of x on y. 1.67 inverts the formula (10/6). 2.2 is the intercept ȳ − 0.6x̄, not the slope.

questions.q: A regression of y on x gives β̂₁ = 0.6 and R² = 0.6. Which statement is correct?
options: A one-unit increase in x causes y to rise by 0.6 in every case
The sample correlation between x and y is 0.6
60% of the sample variation in y is explained by its linear relationship with x
x causes 60% of the value of y
questions.why: R² is the share of the variation in y around its mean that the fitted line explains. The claim about a one-unit increase confuses R² with the slope and also asserts causation, which needs E[u | x] = 0. In simple regression R² is the squared correlation, so the correlation is √0.6 ≈ 0.77, not 0.6. R² says nothing about what fraction of y's level x causes.

questions.q: Explain the zero conditional mean assumption E[u | x] = 0 in the model wage = β₀ + β₁educ + u. Give one reason it may fail, and say in which direction β̂₁ is likely to be biased.
markScheme: States that the average of unobserved factors does not vary with educ
Explains it is needed for unbiasedness of OLS (E[β̂₁] = β₁)
Gives an omitted factor, e.g. ability, in u
Argues ability raises wages and is positively correlated with education
Concludes β̂₁ likely biased upwards (overstates return to education)
questions.modelAnswer: E[u | educ] = 0 means that the average of all unobserved influences on wages is the same at every education level, so educ is unrelated to the error. Together with linearity, random sampling and variation in educ, it guarantees E[β̂₁] = β₁. It is likely to fail because innate ability sits in u: ability raises wages and people with higher ability tend to stay in education longer, so u is positively correlated with educ. OLS then attributes some of ability's effect to education, so β̂₁ is likely to overstate the true return (upward omitted variable bias).

questions.q:
Each of 400 customers entering a shop buys something with probability 0.2, independently of the others. Let N be the number who buy.
(a) State the distribution of N and find its mean and variance. [4]
(b) Use the central limit theorem, with a continuity correction, to approximate P(N ≥ 90). [5]
(c) Use Chebyshev's inequality to bound P(|N − 80| ≥ 16) and compare with the normal approximation. [4]
(d) On another day, 92 of 400 customers buy. Give an approximate 95% confidence interval for the purchase probability p, and test H₀: p = 0.2 against H₁: p ≠ 0.2 at the 5% level. [7]
markScheme: (a) N ~ Binomial(400, 0.2) with justification (fixed n, independence, constant p)
(c) k = 2, bound 1/4; normal gives about 0.0455; comment that Chebyshev is valid for any distribution but conservative
(d) Test statistic uses null SE √(0.2 × 0.8/400) = 0.02: z = 1.5
(d) |z| < 1.96 (p ≈ 0.134), so do not reject H₀; consistent with 0.2 lying inside the CI
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Each customer is a Bernoulli trial with success probability 0.2, there is a fixed number of trials (400) and they are independent, so N ~ Binomial(400, 0.2). E[N] = np = 80 and Var(N) = np(1 − p) = 400 × 0.2 × 0.8 = 64, so SD(N) = 8.

(b) N is a sum of 400 iid Bernoulli variables, so by the CLT it is approximately N(80, 64). With a continuity correction, P(N ≥ 90) ≈ P(Y ≥ 89.5) = P(Z ≥ (89.5 − 80)/8) = P(Z ≥ 1.1875) ≈ 1 − 0.8825 = 0.118. (Without the correction, z = 1.25 gives about 0.106; the exact binomial value is about 0.12, so the corrected figure is closer.)

(c) 16 = 2 standard deviations, so Chebyshev gives P(|N − 80| ≥ 16) ≤ 1/2² = 0.25. The normal approximation gives P(|Z| ≥ 2) ≈ 0.0455. The Chebyshev figure is far larger because it must hold for every distribution with mean 80 and variance 64; it is a guaranteed upper bound, not an estimate.

(d) p̂ = 92/400 = 0.23. The estimated standard error is √(0.23 × 0.77/400) = √0.000443 ≈ 0.0210. A 95% CI is 0.23 ± 1.96 × 0.0210 = 0.23 ± 0.041, i.e. about (0.189, 0.271).
For the test, under H₀ the standard error is √(0.2 × 0.8/400) = 0.02, so z = (0.23 − 0.20)/0.02 = 1.5. The two-sided p-value is 2(1 − Φ(1.5)) ≈ 0.134. As |z| = 1.5 < 1.96, we do not reject H₀ at 5%: the data are consistent with p = 0.2. This agrees with the interval, which contains 0.2.

questions.q:
A researcher regresses log hourly wage (y) on years of schooling (x) for n = 50 workers. Summary statistics: x̄ = 12, ȳ = 2.5, Σ(xᵢ − x̄)² = 400, Σ(xᵢ − x̄)(yᵢ − ȳ) = 32, Σ(yᵢ − ȳ)² = 10, and the sum of squared residuals is SSR = 7.44.
(a) Compute the OLS estimates β̂₀ and β̂₁ and interpret β̂₁. [5]
(b) Compute R² and interpret it. [3]
(c) Estimate σ², find se(β̂₁), and test H₀: β₁ = 0 against H₁: β₁ ≠ 0 at 5% (t₄₈ critical value 2.011). Give a 95% confidence interval for β₁. [7]
(d) Discuss whether β̂₁ is likely to measure the causal effect of schooling on wages. [5]
markScheme: (a) Interpretation: an extra year of schooling is associated with about 8% higher hourly wages (exactly 100(e^0.08 − 1) ≈ 8.3%)
(b) R² = 1 − 7.44/10 = 0.256: schooling explains about a quarter of the sample variation in log wages
(c) t ≈ 4.06 > 2.011: reject H₀ at 5%
(d) Causal interpretation needs E[u | x] = 0; ability (and family background) are omitted, likely positively correlated with schooling, so upward bias; other issues such as measurement error noted
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) β̂₁ = Σ(x − x̄)(y − ȳ)/Σ(x − x̄)² = 32/400 = 0.08. β̂₀ = ȳ − β̂₁x̄ = 2.5 − 0.08 × 12 = 1.54. The fitted equation is log(wage) = 1.54 + 0.08 × schooling. Because y is in logs, one more year of schooling is associated with roughly 8% higher hourly wages (more precisely 100(e^0.08 − 1) ≈ 8.3%).

(b) R² = 1 − SSR/SST = 1 − 7.44/10 = 0.256. Schooling accounts for about 26% of the sample variation in log wages; most of the variation is due to other factors. (Check: the explained sum of squares is β̂₁² × 400 = 0.0064 × 400 = 2.56, and 2.56/10 = 0.256.)

(c) σ̂² = SSR/(n − 2) = 7.44/48 = 0.155. Under homoskedasticity, Var(β̂₁) is estimated by σ̂²/Σ(x − x̄)² = 0.155/400 = 0.000388, so se(β̂₁) ≈ 0.0197.
H₀: β₁ = 0 against H₁: β₁ ≠ 0. t = 0.08/0.0197 ≈ 4.06. Under H₀ (with normal errors) t ~ t₄₈, and |4.06| > 2.011, so we reject H₀ at the 5% level: schooling is statistically significantly associated with wages.
95% CI: 0.08 ± 2.011 × 0.0197 = 0.08 ± 0.0396, i.e. about (0.040, 0.120). It excludes 0, consistent with the test.

(d) β̂₁ is an unbiased estimate of the causal effect only if E[u | schooling] = 0. That is doubtful. Unobserved ability affects wages directly and is probably positively correlated with years of schooling, so it sits in u and is correlated with x. OLS then credits schooling with part of ability's effect, biasing β̂₁ upwards. Family background and motivation raise similar concerns. On the other hand, measurement error in reported schooling would tend to bias the estimate towards zero. With n = 50 the estimate is also imprecise (the CI runs from about 4% to 12%). So the 8% figure is best read as a conditional association; a causal estimate would need a research design that deals with omitted variables, for example a natural experiment or instrumental variables, which you will meet in later econometrics.
